title: The pilot that tried to do everything
scenario:
You work in the transformation office of a hotel group with 40 hotels. The steering group approved a pilot for AI replies to online guest reviews. The scored use case was narrow: draft replies to reviews in English for the guest relations team, who approve each reply.

A project manager wrote the pilot plan in the exhibit. Your director asks you to fix it before Monday's kick-off.
exhibit:
Pilot plan v1 (made-up example data)

Name      "AI for Guest Experience"
Scope     All 40 hotels, all languages. Review replies, plus
          booking emails, plus front-desk chat, plus
          complaint refunds
Length    "Until it works"
Success   "Guests and staff are happy with the AI"
Testing   Go live on day 1; check results at the end
Access    Shared with all 2,600 staff
Budget    No cap set on the API account
Decision  Steering group to discuss at the end

questions.prompt: What is the biggest problem with the scope?

options.text: Forty hotels is too few, so the pilot should include partner hotels as well.
options.explanation: More hotels makes the pilot bigger, not clearer. The problem is that it is already too wide.

options.text: It mixes four different tasks and every hotel and language, so no result can show what worked.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says to start simple and add complexity only when it demonstrably helps. Scope it to English review replies, a few hotels and a fixed time.

options.text: Review replies are too simple for a pilot, so the plan should start with complaint refunds.
options.explanation: Refunds were not the scored use case, and they involve money. Starting there adds risk without a reason.

options.text: The name should be changed to sound more ambitious, so that staff take the pilot seriously.
options.explanation: A name doesn't change what the pilot can prove. The problem is what the pilot tries to cover.

questions.prompt: Which success criteria should replace "guests and staff are happy"?

options.text: "85% of drafts approved with small or no edits; replies within 24 hours; no wrong facts."
options.explanation: Right. Each one is specific and measurable, and together they cover quality, speed and serious errors, as Anthropic's success criteria guide suggests.

options.text: "Staff say in a meeting at the end that the AI replies seem to be working well for the hotels."
options.explanation: OpenAI's evaluation guide calls this a vibe-based eval and lists it as an anti-pattern.

options.text: "Every single reply is perfect and no guest ever complains about a reply again, in any hotel."
options.explanation: Anthropic's guide says targets should be achievable. "Perfect" and "ever" can't be met or measured.

options.text: "The AI writes replies as fast as possible, in as many languages as possible, for all reviews."
options.explanation: "As fast as possible" has no number, and it ignores quality. It also widens the scope again.

questions.prompt: The plan says "go live on day 1". What should happen first?

options.text: Nothing. Live data is the only real test, so earlier testing on past work wastes time.
options.explanation: Live tests matter, but testing on past work first catches problems before guests see them.

options.text: Ask the vendor for its general test scores on public benchmarks, and use those as the result.
options.explanation: Public scores don't use your reviews, your hotels or your tone. They can't tell you if this task works.

options.text: Run the AI on all of last year's reviews and publish the replies, to see how guests react.
options.explanation: Publishing old replies is still going live, with no check before guests see them.

options.text: Draft replies for past reviews that already have approved replies, including hard ones.
options.explanation: Right. Both vendors' guides say to test on realistic cases, including edge cases, and compare with known good answers before going live.

questions.prompt: Which change to access and budget fits a pilot best?

options.text: Keep access open for all 2,600 staff, so the pilot gets as much feedback as it possibly can.
options.explanation: Feedback from people outside the pilot task adds noise, and wide access raises risk. Keep it to the pilot group.

options.text: Remove the budget line, because a pilot is small and API costs can't grow much.
options.explanation: With no cap, nothing stops spend from growing. OpenAI's production guide describes spend limits for this reason.

options.text: Share it only with the pilot team; use a separate project with spend alerts and a hard limit.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's production guide suggests separate projects with their own limits, spend alerts and hard spend limits.

options.text: Give each hotel its own copy of the AI, so that every hotel can change it as it likes.
options.explanation: Forty versions changing at once make results impossible to compare. A pilot needs one setup.
